positions.text: City-funded legal aid to help immigrant families stay together
Local police holding people for ICE without a judge's warrant

c1.quote: Our police should focus on local safety. I'd fund a legal-aid office for immigrant families.
c1.realWorldImpact: The city budget would include roughly $1.2M a year for legal aid and outreach. Local police would limit honoring federal detainer requests without a judicial warrant.

positions.text: Local police cooperating with ICE detainer requests under federal law
Spending city money on immigrant legal services

c2.quote: The city should follow federal law and not spend local dollars on federal responsibilities.
c2.source: Mayoral Debate, League of Voters Forum
c2.realWorldImpact: No new city spending on immigrant legal services would be added to the budget. Local police would continue to honor federal detainer requests under existing practice.

issues.name: Public Transit Funding
issues.description: How much city money should go to buses, light rail and road repair.

positions.text: Doubling bus frequency on every major corridor
The city paying for transit expansion

c1.quote: We will double bus frequency on every major corridor, and the city will pay for it.
c1.source: Mayoral Debate, League of Voters Forum
c1.realWorldImpact: Expect more frequent buses and new routes, funded partly by a proposed 0.25% sales tax increase. Commuters without cars gain the most, while everyone pays slightly more at the register.

positions.text: Riders and private partners covering transit costs
Citywide taxes to fund transit

c2.quote: Riders and private partners should carry transit costs, not every taxpayer in the city.
c2.realWorldImpact: Local taxes would likely stay flat, but bus fares could rise and low-ridership routes may be cut. Service would depend more on private contractors and ridership revenue.

issues.name: Affordable Housing
issues.description: Whether the city should build or subsidize housing, or loosen zoning so private builders add supply.

positions.text: A housing bond for income-restricted homes
Allowing taller buildings near transit stations

c1.quote: I support a housing bond, paired with zoning reform near transit stations.
c1.realWorldImpact: A voter-approved bond would add a small amount to property tax bills to fund income-restricted units. Some neighborhoods near transit would see taller buildings permitted.

positions.text: Faster permits so private builders add housing
City subsidies for housing

c2.quote: Cut the permit backlog and let builders build. Supply is the answer, not subsidies.
c2.realWorldImpact: Permits would move faster and fees could drop, which may increase new market-rate housing. There would be little direct city spending on income-restricted units.

issues.name: Public Safety Budget
issues.description: How the district's share of public safety dollars should be split between police, fire and community programs.

positions.text: Keeping police patrol staffing at current levels
Mental-health responders for non-violent 911 calls

c3.quote: Keep patrol staffing level and add mental-health responders for non-violent calls.
c3.realWorldImpact: A new crisis-response team would take some 911 calls currently handled by officers. This adds about $800K to the city budget without cutting patrol positions.

positions.text: Funding two more fire crews
New programs before response times improve

c4.quote: Response times come first. Fund two more fire crews before any new programs.
c4.realWorldImpact: Fire and EMS response times in District 1 would likely improve. Funding would be shifted from other discretionary programs instead of raising taxes.

positions.text: Better dispatch technology to stretch the current budget
Growing the public safety budget

c5.quote: We can get more from the budget we have through better dispatch technology.
c5.realWorldImpact: Overall public safety spending would stay roughly flat. Improvements would come from software and process changes rather than new staff.

issues.name: Flood & Stormwater Infrastructure
issues.description: Upgrading drainage in flood-prone blocks, and who pays for it.

positions.text: A citywide stormwater fee on utility bills

c3.quote: Flooding is a citywide problem and should be paid for citywide.
c3.realWorldImpact: A new stormwater fee of about $6 a month would appear on utility bills. Flood-prone streets would be prioritized for drainage upgrades within five years.

positions.text: Fixing the ten worst-flooding blocks with existing funds
A new stormwater fee for now

c4.quote: Fix the worst ten blocks now with existing capital funds, then reassess.
c4.realWorldImpact: No new fee in the short term, with targeted repairs funded from the current capital budget. Other planned capital projects could be delayed to cover it.

positions.text: A dedicated stormwater utility, funded by a fee and a bond

c5.quote: I've designed these systems. We need a full stormwater utility, bonded and built in one go.
c5.realWorldImpact: A dedicated stormwater utility would be created with a monthly fee and a bond issue. Construction would be faster and broader, with higher upfront cost to households and businesses.

issues.name: Small Business Taxes & Incentives
issues.description: Business license fees and incentives to fill vacant storefronts.

positions.text: Grants for vacant storefronts that hire locally
Paying for them from the existing economic development fund

c6.quote: Targeted grants for storefronts that hire locally, funded by the existing economic development fund.
c6.realWorldImpact: Some vacant storefronts would receive startup grants tied to local hiring. Business taxes would stay at current levels.

positions.text: Dropping the business license fee for businesses under ten employees

c7.quote: Eliminate the business license fee for anyone under ten employees. That's the incentive.
c7.realWorldImpact: Small businesses would save a few hundred dollars a year in fees. The city would lose that revenue, which may require trims elsewhere in the general fund.

issues.name: Education Budget
issues.description: Whether to seek a local school levy to raise teacher pay and reduce class sizes.

positions.text: Putting a school levy on the ballot
Raising teacher pay to keep teachers from leaving

c8.quote: We are losing teachers to neighboring districts. I'll put a levy on the ballot.
c8.realWorldImpact: Homeowners could see about $120 a year added to property taxes if voters approve the levy. Teacher salaries would rise and average class sizes would drop by an estimated two students.

positions.text: An independent audit of district central-office spending
A new school tax before that audit

c9.quote: Before asking taxpayers for more, we need an independent audit of central-office spending.
c9.realWorldImpact: No new school tax would be proposed in the near term. Any raises for teachers would depend on savings found through the audit.

actions.text: Harlow v. Sampleville Housing Authority, requiring hearings before public-housing evictions
State v. Reyes, which allowed evidence from a warrantless phone search

issues.name: Judicial Approach
issues.description: How each candidate says they decide cases.

positions.text: Following past court decisions unless they are clearly wrong
Explaining rulings in plain language

c10.quote: I follow precedent unless it is clearly wrong, and I write opinions people can actually read.
c10.realWorldImpact: Rulings would likely stay close to past decisions, so outcomes in similar cases are more predictable. Fewer sudden changes in how state law is applied.

positions.text: Reading laws by their plain text
Judges adding exceptions the legislature didn't write

c11.quote: A judge's job is to apply the words the legislature passed, not to add exceptions of their own.
c11.realWorldImpact: Rulings would lean on the literal wording of statutes, which can change results where laws are vague. Fixing unclear laws would fall more on the legislature.
